## Abstract

We present multi-wavelength observations and analysis of SN2024iss, a Type IIb supernova (SN IIb) located at $\sim$ 14 Mpc. The first ZTF detection of SN2024iss is $\sim$ 40 minutes after first light (one of the earliest detections of a SN IIb to date) and a Hubble Space Telescope ultraviolet spectrum was obtained at 7 days (the earliest HST UV SN IIb spectrum to date). We estimate an ejecta mass range of $1.1-3.3{\rm M}_{\odot}$ and ${}^{56}\textrm{Ni}$ mass of $0.11\pm 0.01{\rm M}_{\odot}$ from bolometric light curve modeling and He-star model comparisons. We fit shock-cooling emission models to estimate a progenitor radius of $100-320\ {\rm R}_{\odot}$ and envelope mass of $0.07-0.46\ {\rm M}_{\odot}$ . We compare optical/UV spectra to binary progenitor models, which indicate a stripped hydrogen-rich envelope mass of $0.19-0.28\ {\rm M}_{\odot}$ . We use early-time X-ray detections to calculate CSM densities that are consistent with a progenitor mass-loss rate of $5\times 10^{-4}$ M⊙ yr-1( $v_{w}=100\textrm{km}\,\textrm{s}^{-1}$ ) corresponding to 2-5 years pre-explosion. In the UV, we observe strong Mg ii emission extending to 15000 km/s as well as weak P-Cygni profiles of iron-group elements (e.g., Fe, Ti, Al, Ni) present in outer SN ejecta. The overall spectroscopic evolution of SN2024iss is comparable to SNe IIb, but increased brightness at peak is influenced by SN ejecta-CSM interaction. Nebular spectroscopy of SN2024iss at $\sim 260-412$ days reveals multi-peaked forbidden line profiles of O i and Mg i] indicative of inner ejecta asymmetry and/or clumping. We demonstrate the utility of a rich, multi-wavelength dataset for constraining progenitor systems and explosion dynamics of SNe IIb.

## I Introduction

Type II supernovae (SNe II) occur from the core collapse of massive stars ( $\gtrsim 8\ {\rm M}_{\odot}$ ), and are characterized by hydrogen features in their spectra. SNe IIb are a transitional class of SNe II that display hydrogen features in early time spectra, but evolve to be dominated by helium (He i) features in later times as typically seen in Type Ib SNe (A. V. Filippenko, 1997). These features are often attributed to the progenitor possessing a low-mass hydrogen envelope (S. E. Woosley et al., 1994; S. Woosley & T. Janka, 2005; S. Hachinger et al., 2012), indicating high mass-loss rates from the progenitor leading up to its explosion (J. R. Maund et al., 2004; N. Smith et al., 2011; S. Ben-Ami et al., 2015). While not fully understood, this mass-loss can be explained by interactions of the progenitor with a companion star in a binary system (P. Podsiadlowski et al., 1992; J. R. Maund et al., 2004; S.-C. Yoon et al., 2010; S.-C. Yoon et al., 2017; A. Ercolino et al., 2024). Several SNe IIb progenitors have been identified as yellow supergiant stars through direct imaging of the progenitor (e.g., G. Aldering et al. 1994; J. R. Maund et al. 2004; M. C. Bersten et al. 2012; S. D. Van Dyk et al. 2014; A. Reguitti et al. 2025). Previous studies have suggested that yellow supergiant progenitors began their final stages as red supergiants, but evolved to yellow supergiants by the time of explosion due to high mass-loss rates (C. Georgy, 2012).

Surface composition and mass-loss of the progenitor can be explored with early time observations of the SN (A. Gal-Yam et al., 2014). Chemical elements ejected by the progenitor during mass-loss remain in the medium surrounding the star, and are ionized by the shock wave radiation resulting from the collision of SN ejecta and circumstellar material (CSM; O. Yaron et al. 2017; L. Dessart et al. 2017). Evidence of this photoionization can be seen through narrow emission features in ultraviolet spectra of the supernova until $\sim~7$ days after first light (E. A. Zimmerman et al., 2024). Previous studies of early-time UV spectra of SNe II have been successful in tracing progenitor atmospheres, mass-loss, CSM abundance and density, as well as the structure and temperature of the supernova ejecta (S. S. Vasylyev et al., 2022; S. S. Vasylyev et al., 2023; K. A. Bostroem et al., 2023; E. A. Zimmerman et al., 2024, e.g.,).

SN 2024iss was first reported to the Transient Name Server (TNS) by the Gravitational-wave Optical Transient Observer (GOTO; M. J. Dyer et al. 2018; M. J. Dyer et al. 2020) on 2024-05-13 (MJD 60443.03, B. Godson et al. 2024). SN 2024iss was classified as a Type IIb SN (S. Srivastav et al., 2024) and is located at $\alpha=12^{\textrm{h}}59^{\textrm{m}}06.130^{\textrm{s}}$ , $\delta=+28^{\circ}48^{\prime}42.62^{\prime\prime}$ in the host galaxy DESI J194.7752+28.8122. M. Yamanaka et al. (2025) presented estimates of physical parameters of SN 2024iss from its bolometric light curve and blackbody properties, while L. Chen et al. (2025) presented estimates of physical properties through analysis and modeling of optical and UV photometry, optical spectroscopy, and X-ray observations. We present, analyze, and model a range of multi-wavelength data including UV/Optical/NIR photometry, UV/Optical/NIR spectroscopy, and X-ray observations.

The last pre-explosion image of SN 2024iss was by ZTF on MJD 60442.23 ( $m>21.037$ mag in $g$ -band), followed by an intra-night ZTF $i$ -band detection ( $m=16.8$ mag) 1.3 hours later on MJD 60442.28 (see Figure 1). Given the depth of the last non-detection, we constrain the time of first light to be MJD $60442.254\pm 0.0271$ , which is later and more constrained than the explosion epoch reported in L. Chen et al. (2025). We define $\delta t$ throughout as the time since first light in rest-frame days. For SN 2024iss, we use a redshift of $z=0.003238\pm 0.000033$ (DESI Collaboration et al., 2024), which corresponds to a luminosity distance of $14.04\pm 0.14$ Mpc for standard $\Lambda$ CDM cosmology ( $H_{0}$ = 70 km s-1 Mpc-1, $\Omega_{M}=0.27$ , $\Omega_{\Lambda}=0.73$ ). Unfortunately, no redshift-independent distance is available. The main parameters of SN 2024iss and its host galaxy are displayed in Table 1.

Section II describes the observations used in this paper. In Section III we present an analysis of photometric data, including light curve comparisons, shock breakout constraints, blackbody evolution, derivation of the 56Ni mass, and shock cooling emission modeling. In Section IV, we analyze ultraviolet, optical, and NIR spectroscopy with comparisons to model and other SNe IIb spectra. In Section V, we derive the CSM and progenitor mass-loss history through X-ray observations. Finally, our discussion and conclusions are presented in Sections VI and VII.

### II.1 UV/Optical/NIR Photometry

The complete, multi-band light curve of SN 2024iss is presented in Figure 2. SN 2024iss was first detected by the Zwicky Transient Facility (ZTF; E. C. Bellm et al. 2019) in $i$ -band and was subsequently monitored in $gri$ bands. ZTF photometry comes from Public, Partnership and Caltech streams and was generated through the ZTF forced-photometry service (F. J. Masci et al., 2019). Additional $ugri$ band photometry was obtained with the Spectral Energy Distribution Machine (SEDM; N. Blagorodnova et al. 2018) on the 60-in telescope at Palomar Observatory. Data storage and observation follow-up was performed through the SkyPortal interface and the Fritz broker (S. van der Walt et al., 2019; M. W. Coughlin et al., 2023).

SN 2024iss was observed with the Pan-STARRS telescope (N. Kaiser et al., 2002; K. C. Chambers et al., 2016, PS1;) through the Young Supernova Experiment (YSE) (D. O. Jones et al., 2021) between 2024-05-24 and 2025-08-19 ( $\delta t=12.1-464.0$ days since first light). Data storage/visualization and follow-up coordination was done through the YSE-PZ web broker (D. A. Coulter et al., 2022; D. A. Coulter et al., 2023). The YSE photometric pipeline is based on photpipe (A. Rest et al., 2005), which relies on calibrations from E. A. Magnier et al. (2020) and C. Z. Waters et al. (2020). Each image template was taken from stacked PS1 exposures, with most of the input data from the PS1 3 $\pi$ survey (K. C. Chambers et al., 2016). All images and templates were resampled and astrometrically aligned to match a skycell in the PS1 sky tessellation. An image zero-point is determined by comparing PSF photometry of the stars to updated stellar catalogs of PS1 observations (H. A. Flewelling et al., 2016). The PS1 templates are convolved with a three-Gaussian kernel to match the PSF of the nightly images, and the convolved templates are subtracted from the nightly images with HOTPANTS (A. Becker, 2015). Finally, a flux-weighted centroid is found for the position of the SN in each image and PSF photometry is performed using “forced photometry”: the centroid of the PSF is forced to be at the SN position. The nightly zero-point is applied to the photometry to determine the brightness of the SN for that epoch.

We also observed SN 2024iss with the 1-m Lulin telescope in $griz$ bands from 2024-06-25 to 2024-07-17. Standard calibrations for bias and flat-fielding were performed on the images using IRAF (D. Tody, 1986), and we reduced the calibrated frames in photpipe using the same methods described in C. D. Kilpatrick et al. (2018).

The Ultraviolet Optical Telescope (UVOT; P. W. A. Roming et al. 2005) onboard the Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory (N. Gehrels et al., 2004) observed SN 2024iss from 2024-05-13 to 2025-05-03 ( $\delta t=1.51-356.0$ days). We performed aperture photometry with a 5′′ region radius with uvotsource within HEAsoft v6.33 (Nasa High Energy Astrophysics Science Archive Research Center (2014)Nasa High Energy Astrophysics Science Archive Research Center (Heasarc), Heasarc)44 4 We used the most recent calibration database (CALDB) version., following the standard guidelines from P. J. Brown et al. (2014)55 5 https://github.com/gterreran/Swift_host_subtraction. In order to remove contamination from the host galaxy, we employed pre-explosion images to subtract the measured count rate at the location of the SN from the count rates in the SN images and corrected for point-spread-function (PSF) losses following the prescriptions of P. J. Brown et al. (2014).

Near-infrared (NIR) data of SN 2024iss was obtained with the Hiroshima Optical and Near-InfraRed camera (HONIR) instrument of the 1.0-m Kanata Telescope, Hiroshima. The sky-background subtraction was done using a template sky image obtained by dithering individual frames at different positions. We performed PSF photometry and calibrated the SN magnitudes using comparison stars in the 2MASS catalog (S. E. Persson et al., 1998).

### II.2 Reddening and Host Galaxy Properties

The Milky Way (MW) $V$ -band extinction and color excess along the SN line of sight is $A_{V}=0.031$ mag and E(B-V) = 0.01 mag (D. J. Schlegel et al., 1998; E. F. Schlafly & D. P. Finkbeiner, 2011) respectively, which we correct for using a standard E. L. Fitzpatrick (1999) reddening law (assuming $R_{V}$ = 3.1). In addition to the MW color excess, we estimate the contribution of host galaxy extinction in the local SN environment by measuring the equivalent widths (EWs) of each component of the Na i doublet in the medium resolution spectrum from the Palomar Double Spectrograph (DBSP; J. B. Oke & J. E. Gunn 1982). We use $A_{V}^{\rm host}=(0.78\pm 0.15)~{\rm mag}\times({\rm EW_{NaID}}$ /Å) from M. D. Stritzinger et al. (2018) to convert these EWs into to a host-galaxy $E(B-V)$ and derive a host galaxy extinction of $E(B-V)_{\textrm{host}}=0.019\pm 0.004$ mag, also corrected for using the E. L. Fitzpatrick (1999) reddening law.

We utilize a Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS) spectrum to constrain the properties of the dwarf host galaxy of SN 2024iss. In the SDSS spectrum, we find strong H $\alpha$ emission but no significant detections of other typical galaxy lines. We derive upper limits on the line fluxes of H $\beta$ , [O iii] $\lambda 5007$ , and N ii $\lambda 6584$ by simulating a synthetic Gaussian profile with the Full-Width-Half-Maximum (FWHM) set to the spectral resolution until a 3 $\sigma$ detection is recovered above the continuum. However, because only flux limits can be determined for these emission lines, we cannot estimate a reliable limit on the $O3N2$ ratio. Nonetheless, we find $N2=\rm log_{10}(\rm[NII]/H\alpha)<-0.662$ , which corresponds to a limit on the oxygen abundance of $\rm 12+log(O/H)<8.44$ using the relation in R. A. Marino et al. (2013). This oxygen abundance corresponds to a likely sub-solar host galaxy metallicity of $Z<0.6~\rm Z_{\odot}$ .

### II.3 UV/Optical/NIR Spectroscopy

We present our full range of UV, Optical, and NIR spectroscopic observations in Table 2. We obtained 33 optical spectra covering $\delta t=1.1$ to 411.3 days, an $HST$ UV spectrum at $\delta t=7.0$ days, and NIR spectra in both photospheric and nebular phases. We obtained an early-time ultraviolet spectrum of SN 2024iss with the Hubble Space Telescope (HST) Space Telescope Imaging Spectrograph (STIS; B. E. Woodgate et al. (1998)) on 19 May 2024 ( $\delta t=7$ days). The SN was observed through HST Cycle 31 “Flex Thursday” Target of Opportunity Program 17507 (PI: Jacobson-Galán). Spectra were obtained in the G230LB (1680 – 3060 Å), G430L (2900 – 5700 Å), and G750L (5236 – 10266 Å) gratings, resulting in a $\delta t=7$ day spectrum ranging from 1680 – 10266 Å. We reduced the spectra using the stistools package by performing cosmic ray rejection, matching the extraction aperture size across the gratings, increasing the local background size, and placing the local background closer to the spectral trace.

We obtained optical spectra of SN 2024iss with the Kast spectrograph on the 3-m Shane telescope at Lick Observatory (J. S. Miller & R. P. S. Stone, 1993). For all of these spectroscopic observations, standard CCD processing and spectrum extraction were accomplished with IRAF66 6 https://github.com/msiebert1/UCSC_spectral_pipeline. The data was extracted using the optimal algorithm of K. Horne (1986). Low-order polynomial fits to calibration-lamp spectra were used to establish the wavelength scale and apply small adjustments derived from night-sky lines in the object frames. Additional optical spectra of SN 2024iss were also obtained with the Palomar Spectral Energy Distribution Machine (SEDM; N. Blagorodnova et al. 2018; Y.-L. Kim et al. 2022), the Alhambra Faint Object Spectrograph and Camera (ALFOSC)77 7 http://www.not.iac.es/instruments/alfosc, the Spectrograph for the Rapid Acquisition of Transients (SPRAT; A. S. Piascik et al. 2014), and DBSP. Late-time optical spectra were obtained with the Low Resolution Imaging Spectrometer (LRIS; J. B. Oke et al. 1995) on the 10-m Keck I telescope and reduced with Lpipe (D. A. Perley, 2019). Near-infrared (NIR) spectra were obtained with the $R\approx 2700$ Near-Infrared Echelle Spectrograph (NIRES; J. C. Wilson et al. 2004) located on the 10-m Keck II telescope. The data were reduced using a custom version of the IDL based reduction package Spextool (M. C. Cushing et al., 2004) modified for use with NIRES as well as the Pypeit spectral reduction pipeline (J. Prochaska et al., 2020). For the Spextool reduction, we used xtellcor (W. D. Vacca et al., 2003) to correct for telluric features in our spectrum using an A0 standard star observed close in airmass and time to our target. NIRES data were obtained through the Keck Infrared Transient Survey (KITS; S. Tinyanont et al. 2024). A complete log of spectroscopic observations is presented in Table 2.

### II.4 X-ray Observations & Comparisons

The X-Ray Telescope (XRT, D. N. Burrows et al. 2005) on board the Swift spacecraft (N. Gehrels et al., 2004) observed the field of SN 2024iss from 2024-05-13 to 2025-05-03 ( $\delta t=1.51-356.0$ days, with a total exposure time of 60 ks). We analyzed the data using XSNAP (Ferdinand et al., 2025) and followed standard filtering and screening prescriptions. A bright source of X-ray emission is clearly detected in each individual observation with significance of $>3\sigma$ against the background in the first seven epochs ( $\delta t=1.51-7.10$ days; total exposure time of 10.7 ks). In order to increase the detection significance, we chose to merge event files in 2 day bins and use the combined epochs for analysis of the X-ray spectrum. Similar to the X-ray evolution reported in L. Chen et al. (2025), we find a significant decrease in X-ray luminosity at $\delta t>8.88$ days. A complete log of Swift-XRT observations is presented in Table 3 and 4.

From each merged event file, we extracted a spectrum using a 25′′ region centered at the location of SN 2024iss and corrected for background emission with a 100′′ source-free region. We use Xspec to model each 0.3-10 keV spectra with an absorbed thermal bremsstrahlung model (tbabs*ztbabs*bremss), which includes solar abundances (M. Asplund et al., 2009), and a line-of-sight hydrogen column density of $N_{\rm H,MW}=1.1\times 10^{20}$ cm-2. We are unable to constrain the temperature in our model fits so we adopt a forward shock temperature evolution following the self-similar solutions by R. A. Chevalier (1982) and R. A. Chevalier & C. Fransson (2017). Here, temperature goes as $T_{\rm FS}(t)\propto t^{2(s-3)(n-s)}$ , and we adopt $s=2$ for a “wind-like” CSM and outer ejecta profile index of $n=10$ . This is based on what is commonly adopted for SNe IIb that are thought to arise from more extended progenitors (e.g., see C. Fransson et al. 1996; T. K. Nymark et al. 2009; P. Chandra et al. 2009; A. Kamble et al. 2016). We normalize the X-ray temperature evolution to be $T=33\ \rm keV\ (t/5d)^{-0.25}$ based on the temperature measurement presented by L. Chen et al. (2025) using NuSTAR observations (R. Margutti et al., 2024).

We present the 0.3-10 keV luminosities and derived upper limits in Figure 3, with all best-fit model parameters and flux measurements being presented in Table 4. Compared to other SNe IIb, SN 2024iss is more luminous than SNe 2011dh (A. M. Soderberg et al., 2012) and 2016gkg (R. Margutti et al., 2016) at $\delta t<7$ days. Similarly, SN 2024iss is also brighter in X-rays than CSM-interacting SNe II-P 2023ixf (B. W. Grefenstette et al., 2023; P. Chandra et al., 2024; A. J. Nayana et al., 2025) and 2024ggi (Ferdinand et al., 2025). However, the X-ray light curve of SN 2024iss fades significantly more dramatically than SNe IIb 1993J (P. Chandra et al., 2009) and 2013df (A. Kamble et al., 2016) at $\delta t>7$ days. The earliest detections of SN 2024iss are also fainter than H-free SNe e.g., SNe 2008D, 2019ehk, 2021gno (A. M. Soderberg et al., 2008; M. Modjaz et al., 2009; W. V. Jacobson-Galán et al., 2020; W. V. Jacobson-Galán et al., 2022). The X-ray light curve evolution and its connection to confined CSM in SN 2024iss is discussed in Section V.

### III.1 Light Curve

The multiband light curve of SN 2024iss (see Figure 2) shows two prominent peaks (as seen in Figure 4). We refer to the primary as the shock cooling peak, which can be seen in all optical and ultraviolet bands, with a peak $g$ absolute magnitude 88 8 All absolute magnitudes include extinction correction (see Section II.1) of $-17.584\pm 0.022$ mag at $\delta t=2.24$ days. We calculated this peak by fitting a third-order polynomial to $g$ -band photometry between $\delta t=1-4$ days. Similarly, we fit a third-order polynomial to $g$ -band photometry between $\delta t=3-10$ days to find the minimum between the two peaks, which has an absolute magnitude of $-16.972\pm 0.022$ mag at $\delta t=7.01$ days. The second peak, ranging from $\delta t=\sim 7-40$ days in the $g$ -band, results from radiation during the decay chain of ${}^{56}\mathrm{Ni}\rightarrow^{56}\mathrm{Co}\rightarrow^{56}\mathrm{Fe}$ , synthesized in the inner ejecta of the supernova (W. D. Arnett, 1980). The ${}^{56}\mathrm{Ni}$ peak is seen most prominently in the optical bands, with a peak $g$ absolute magnitude of $-17.469\pm 0.022$ mag at $\delta t=16.77$ days. We calculated this peak by fitting a third-order polynomial to $g$ -band photometry between $\delta t=10-30$ days. Since the host galaxy is nearby, we note that there may be additional uncertainty in the redshift measurement and the resulting redshift-dependent distance calculation. To account for this, we calculate the following $g$ -band peak absolute magnitudes for the second light curve peak for a distance uncertainty of $\pm 5$ Mpc: at a distance of 9 Mpc, $M^{\textrm{peak}}_{g}=-16.504$ mag, and at a distance of 19 Mpc, $M^{\textrm{peak}}_{g}=-18.127$ mag. This uncertainty may propagate into the physical parameters derived from photometric data in Section III. However, due to the lack of constraints on this uncertainty, we adopt the redshift-dependent distance of $14.04\pm 0.14$ Mpc for further analysis.

We compare the light curve of SN 2024iss with other prototypical SNe IIb (1993J, 2011dh, 2013df, 2016gkg) and the upcoming complete ZTF SNe IIb sample from Hinds et al., in prep (see Figure 4). Photometry in the $r$ -band (1993J: S. E. Woosley et al. 1994; 2011dh: M. C. Bersten et al. 2012; 2013df: A. Morales-Garoffolo et al. 2014; 2016gkg: L. Tartaglia et al. 2017; C. D. Kilpatrick et al. 2017; M. C. Bersten et al. 2018) reveals SN 2024iss to have a similar magnitude shock cooling peak but a brighter second peak from 56Ni decay. Additionally, the transition between the first and second peaks of the light curve is less pronounced in SN 2024iss compared to the other SNe (see Section V discussion on how CSM interaction impacts this observable).

### III.2 Shock Breakout Constraints

As shown in Figures 1 & 7, the time of first light in SN 2024iss is tightly bracketed between the last ZTF $g$ -band non-detection on MJD 60442.23 and first ZTF $i$ -band detection on MJD 60442.28. Consequently, the uncertainty on time of first light is empirically constrained to $\pm 40$ min, assuming first light is when the SN is brighter than $M_{g}>-9.8$ mag, which reflects the limiting magnitude of the last $g$ -band non-detection. As shown in the right panel of Figure 7, we jointly fit the $gri$ -band photometry at $\delta t<2$ days using the following power-law formalism:

$$ F_{\nu}(t)=\begin{cases}a(t-t_{\mathrm{fl}})^{b}&\text{if }t\geq t_{\mathrm{fl}}\\
0&\text{if }t<t_{\mathrm{fl}}\end{cases} $$

where $a$ and $b$ can vary across filters but $t_{fl}$ remains fixed (e.g., see A. A. Miller et al. 2020; N. Rehemtulla et al. 2025). We first fit the light curves with the earliest $i$ -band point excluded, which unsurprisingly leads to a time of first light that is too late in time to be consistent with the last non-detection and first detection of SN 2024iss. Second, we fit with first light fixed to be the phase of the last $g$ -band non-detection and force a consistent temperature evolution wherein $F_{\nu,\ g}>F_{\nu,\ r}>F_{\nu,\ i}$ (shown as dashed lines in Fig. 7). Overall, the power law indices across filters are consistent with thermal SN emission where bluer filters are more sensitive to decreasing temperature and rise slower than redder filters i.e., $a_{g}<a_{r}$ . However, even when first light is fixed to the last non-detection date, this single index power law model cannot reproduce the flux observed in the earliest $i$ -band detection, which deviates from the model at a $\sim 44~\sigma$ level. A similar early light curve evolution was observed in type II SNe 2023ixf and 2024ggi, both of which showed evidence for delayed shock breakout from dense CSM given the need for multiple powerlaw components when fitting their observed photometry in the first $\sim$ day after first light (G. Hosseinzadeh et al., 2023; G. Li et al., 2024; M. Shrestha et al., 2024; W. V. Jacobson-Galán et al., 2024). Therefore, by using the last non-detection in $g$ -band and first photometry points consistent with the power law model, we can constrain the regime of shock breakout emission to be $\delta t<0.42$ day, where the first $i$ -band detection is likely associated with shock breakout.

We can further constrain the shock breakout emission in SN 2024iss by considering the expected energy, temperature and various timescales that are at play for massive star breakout emission. For a typical SN IIb progenitor with envelope mass and radius of $M_{e}=0.1~{\rm M}_{\odot}$ and $R_{e}=300~{\rm R}_{\odot}$ , the amount of energy that travels through this envelope at breakout can be expressed as:

$$ E_{e}\approx 1.3\times 10^{50}\Bigg(\frac{E_{k}}{10^{51}\rm\ erg}\Bigg)\Bigg(\frac{M_{c}}{2\ \rm{\rm M}_{\odot}}\Bigg)^{-0.7}\Bigg(\frac{M_{e}}{0.1\ \rm{\rm M}_{\odot}}\Bigg)^{0.7}\rm erg $$

where $E_{k}$ is the SN kinetic energy and $M_{c}$ is the core mass (E. Nakar & A. L. Piro, 2014). Treating this as a low energy SN in an extended envelope we can use the relations for a $n=3/2$ polytrope from C. D. Matzner & C. F. McKee (1999) to express the shock breakout radiation temperature as:

$$ \displaystyle T_{\rm SBO}=6.2\times 10^{5}\left(\frac{E_{e}}{1.3\times 10^{50}\ {\rm erg}}\right)^{0.20} \displaystyle\left(\frac{M_{e}}{0.1\,M_{\odot}}\right)^{-0.052}\left(\frac{R_{e}}{300\,R_{\odot}}\right)^{-0.54}\ {\rm K} $$

where we assume $\kappa=0.34$ cm2 g-1 and $\rho/\rho_{\star}=1$ . Then the total energy in shock breakout goes as:

$$ \displaystyle E_{\rm SBO}=1.7\times 10^{48}\left(\frac{E_{e}}{1.3\times 10^{50}\ {\rm erg}}\right)^{0.56} \displaystyle\left(\frac{M_{e}}{0.1\,M_{\odot}}\right)^{-0.44}\left(\frac{R_{e}}{300\,R_{\odot}}\right)^{1.74}\ {\rm erg} $$

The total luminosity depends on the timescales over which photons are observed. According to C. D. Matzner & C. F. McKee (1999), the diffusion timescale goes as:

$$ \displaystyle t_{\rm diff}\approx 500\left(\frac{E_{e}}{1.3\times 10^{50}\ {\rm erg}}\right)^{-0.79} \displaystyle\left(\frac{M_{e}}{0.1\,M_{\odot}}\right)^{0.21}\left(\frac{R_{e}}{300\,R_{\odot}}\right)^{2.16}\ {\rm s} $$

Additionally, the light travel timescale can be expressed as:

$$ \displaystyle t_{\rm lt}=\frac{R_{e}}{c}=700\left(\frac{R_{e}}{300\,R_{\odot}}\right)\ {\rm s} $$

Finally, for the non-spherical effect timescale ( $t_{\rm nsph}\approx\frac{R_{e}}{v_{\rm sh}}$ ), we can express the shock velocity as:

$$ \displaystyle v_{\rm sh}\approx 3.5\times 10^{9}\left(\frac{E_{e}}{1.3\times 10^{50}\ {\rm erg}}\right)^{0.57} \displaystyle\left(\frac{M_{e}}{0.1\,M_{\odot}}\right)^{-0.44}\left(\frac{R_{e}}{300\,R_{\odot}}\right)^{-0.26}\ {\rm cm\ s^{-1}} $$

This then allows us to describe the non-spherical timescale as:

$$ \displaystyle t_{\rm nsph}\approx\frac{R_{e}}{v_{\rm sh}}\approx 6\times 10^{3}\left(\frac{E_{e}}{1.3\times 10^{50}\ {\rm erg}}\right)^{-0.57} \displaystyle\left(\frac{M_{e}}{0.1\,M_{\odot}}\right)^{0.44}\left(\frac{R_{e}}{300\,R_{\odot}}\right)^{1.26}\ {\rm s} $$

Given our fiducial SN IIb values, the diffusion timescale is likely insignificant and shock breakout is defined by light travel time and non-spherical effects i.e., $t_{\rm SBO}\approx 12\rm\min-2\ hrs$ . Assuming that shock breakout occurs directly after the last ZTF non-detection, the first $i$ -band detection at 1.3 hrs later does lie within this shock breakout time window, and would be more consistent with non-spherical effects, which are known to elongate the shock breakout signal in massive stars when calcuated in 3-D simulations (e.g., see J. A. Goldberg et al. 2022).

### III.3 Blackbody Evolution

We calculated the bolometric light curve of SN 2024iss based on photometry interpolated from the UVW2, UVM2, UVW1, and $UBgVriz$ bands up to $\delta t=50$ days using the superbol package (M. Nicholl, 2018). A blackbody spectral energy distribution was fit to the interpolated observations, resulting in calculations for the bolometric luminosity, blackbody temperature, and blackbody radius for each epoch (see Figure 5 left panel). The bolometric luminosity shows the same double-peaked shape as the observed photometry. The highest temperature of $(2.09\pm 0.45)\times 10^{4}$ K occurs at $\delta t=1.05$ days and the peak bolometric luminosity is $(1.03\pm 0.70)\times 10^{43}$ erg s ${}^{-1}\ \ (\textrm{log}_{L_{\textrm{bol}}}=43.01)$ at $\delta t=2.10$ days. The peak temperature is higher than that of SN 2016gkg ( $\sim 10,000$ K at $\delta t=1.70$ days; L. Tartaglia et al. 2017) and lower than that of SN 1993J ( $\sim 10^{5}$ K; S. E. Woosley et al. 1994), while the bolometric luminosity is comparable to other IIb SNe (M. C. Bersten et al., 2012; A. Morales-Garoffolo et al., 2014; L. Tartaglia et al., 2017).

From these parameters, we calculated a blackbody spectrum at $\delta t=7$ days, and compared it to the observed $\delta t=7$ days HST spectrum and observed photometry at similar phases (see Figure 6). For this phase, we only consider interpolated photometry from the $i$ to UVW2 bands since there are no $z$ -band observations in the earliest phases. The overall shape of both spectra match well, indicating a $\delta t=7$ days blackbody temperature of $8,660\pm 130$ K and a blackbody radius of $(8.3\pm 0.2)\times 10^{14}$ cm. To quantify the departure from a thermal continuum, we compute the root mean square (RMS) fractional deviation between the observed spectrum and the best-fit blackbody model over various wavelength ranges. At optical wavelengths ( $3000-9000$ Å), the flux uncertainty weighted RMS deviation is 9%, which increases to 17% across near-UV wavelengths ( $1600-3000$ Å). Interestingly, the RMS deviation from $1600-2200$ Å reaches 47%, which can be observed visually in Figure 6 as the blackbody continuum drops sharply at $<2200$ Å compared to emission/absorption profiles from Fe-group elements SN 2024iss.

### III.4 56Ni Mass Estimation

In order to infer ejecta mass ( $M_{\rm ej}$ ), kinetic energy ( $E_{\rm k}$ ), and ${}^{56}\textrm{Ni}$ mass ( $M_{\textrm{Ni}}$ ), we fit the SN 2024iss bolometric light curve with a two-component model presented in Appendix A of S. Valenti et al. (2008) and in J. C. Wheeler et al. (2015) (see Figure 5 right panel). This analytic formalism distinguishes between photospheric ( $\delta t<30$ days; W. D. Arnett 1982) and nebular ( $\delta t>40$ days; P. G. Sutherland & J. C. Wheeler 1984; E. Cappellaro et al. 1997) phases of the light curve and implements the possibility of incomplete $\gamma$ -ray trapping and a typical opacity of $\kappa=0.1$ cm2 g-1. Given the known degeneracy between $E_{\rm k}$ and $M_{\rm ej}$ , we adopt a photospheric velocity of $v_{\rm ph}\approx 6500~\textrm{km}\,\textrm{s}^{-1}$ based on the Fe ii absorption minimum at peak brightness. For the photospheric model ( $10<\delta t<30$ days), we fit the secondary light curve peak and find an ejecta mass of $M_{\rm ej}=1.1\pm 0.1~{\rm M}_{\odot}$ , kinetic energy of $E_{\rm k}=(2.6\pm 0.3)\times 10^{50}$ erg, and ${}^{56}\textrm{Ni}$ mass of $M_{\textrm{Ni}}=0.11\pm 0.01~{\rm M}_{\odot}$ . However, this $E_{k}$ value is nonphysical given the large ejecta velocities ( $\sim 15{,}000-18{,}000~\textrm{km}\,\textrm{s}^{-1}$ ) of the fastest moving SN ejecta observed in the SN spectra at $\delta t\sim 3$ days (e.g., see Fig. 10). We note that using these “Arnett-like” formalisms fit H-poor SNe at peak can over-estimate the ${}^{56}\textrm{Ni}$ mass by up to $\sim$ 50% (e.g., see L. Dessart et al. 2015; L. Dessart et al. 2016; N. Afsariardchi et al. 2021; A. Haynie & A. L. Piro 2023). However, we compare the rise-time and luminosity at peak in SN 2024iss to radioactive decay model light curves calibrated with numerical radiation transport simulations presented in D. K. Khatami & D. N. Kasen (2019) and find that $M_{\textrm{Ni}}$ is likely $\sim 0.09-0.1~{\rm M}_{\odot}$ .

For the nebular phase model ( $\delta t>30$ days), we find a larger kinetic energy of $E_{\rm k}=(6.3\pm 0.1)\times 10^{50}$ erg and, consequently, a larger ejecta mass of $M_{\rm ej}=2.5\pm 0.03~{\rm M}_{\odot}$ . We find a ${}^{56}\textrm{Ni}$ mass estimated from the nebular phase model to be $M_{\textrm{Ni}}=0.11\pm 0.01~{\rm M}_{\odot}$ , similar to the photospheric model estimate. Additionally, we fit the bolometric light curve from $\delta t=60-300$ days with a radioactive decay model that has the timescale of $\gamma$ -ray escape during energy disposition from ${}^{56}\textrm{Co}$ decay ( $t_{\gamma}$ ) and $M_{\textrm{Ni}}$ as free parameters (P. G. Sutherland & J. C. Wheeler, 1984; A. Clocchiatti & J. C. Wheeler, 1997; J. C. Wheeler et al., 2015; W. V. Jacobson-Galán et al., 2021). We find a similar ${}^{56}\textrm{Ni}$ mass to the other model formalisms ( $M_{\textrm{Ni}}=0.091\pm 0.002~{\rm M}_{\odot}$ ) and a $\gamma$ -ray leakage timescale of $t_{\gamma}=145.7\pm 2.7$ days, which is similar to other SNe IIb (J. C. Wheeler et al., 2015; A. Haynie & A. L. Piro, 2023). Modeling of the light curve “tail” also provides a consistency check for the parameters derived above using the photospheric model.

### III.5 Shock Cooling Emission Modeling

The first peak in the light curve corresponds to cooling of the extended stellar envelope after the shock from the supernova propagates through it (S. E. Woosley et al., 1994; L. Dessart et al., 2011; M. C. Bersten et al., 2012; E. Nakar & A. L. Piro, 2014; M. C. Bersten et al., 2018). The effects from this phenomenon are visible until emission from the ${}^{56}\mathrm{Ni}$ decay becomes brighter than the fading emission from shocked envelope. In the $g$ -band, the first peak decreases until $\delta t=7$ days, after which the flux begins to increase again. This can also be seen in the bolometric luminosity light curve, in which the second peak begins to rise around $\delta t=8$ days. We modeled photometry in the $i$ , $r$ , $V$ , $g$ , $B$ , $U$ , UVW1, UVM2, and UVW2 bands with the N. Sapir & E. Waxman 2017 (SW17), J. Morag et al. 2023 (MSW23), and A. L. Piro et al. 2021 (P21) shock cooling emission models.

*Figure 6: The observed HST $\delta t=7$ days spectrum with the calculated blackbody spectrum and observed photometry at $\delta t=7$ days. The observed spectrum and photometry are corrected for dust extinction.*

SW17 is a physically calibrated model for red and blue supergiant progenitors based on luminosity from shock cooling emission. In the model, the assumed value of the polytropic index $n$ (related to the density profile of the stellar envelope) differentiates between the red and blue supergiant, with $n=1.5$ taken to represent a red supergiant progenitor with a convective envelope, and $n=3$ a blue supergiant progenitor with a fully radiative envelope. Since type IIb supernovae are especially sensitive to the value of $n$ due to their low envelope masses (J. R. Farah et al., 2025) and the inefficient convection in the progenitor envelopes (J. A. Goldberg et al., 2026), we modeled the shock cooling emission with both versions of SW17 for each $n$ value. MSW23 is an analytic model that builds from the SW17 $n=1.5$ model with a two-phase expansion of the supernova ejecta. Both SW17 and MSW23 approximate a constant opacity during shock cooling emission, which is only valid during times when the supernova temperature is above $8{,}120$ K, according to the model setup described in N. Sapir & E. Waxman (2017). From our bolometric fits (see Section III.3), the blackbody temperature is above this threshold until $\delta t=9$ days. However, due to the rise of emission from ${}^{56}\mathrm{Ni}$ decay, we limit our shock cooling emission fitting to observations to $\delta t<7$ days.

P21 is an analytic model that builds on the low-mass extended material model of A. L. Piro (2015) by incorporating two-zones with varying densities and velocities. We used the Python packages shock-cooling-curve (P. Venkatraman & W. Jacobson-Galán, 2024) to fit P21 and SW17, and lightcurve-fitting (G. Hosseinzadeh et al., 2023) to fit MSW23. We tested fits for each model for photometry up to $\delta t=5$ , 6, and 7 days, and chose the best statistical fit for each model (see Appendix A). As a result, we fit SW17 and MSW23 with photometry up to $\delta t=7$ days and P21 with photometry up to $\delta t=5$ days. Additionally, MSW23 contains a factor for UV flux suppression, $A$ , which we set equal to $1$ (indicating no UV flux suppression) due to the model underestimating flux in the UV bands (see Figure 8). We found best fit parameters using MCMC fitting with 1000 steps and 25 walkers for each model. The results are shown in Table 5. The 4 models result in a progenitor radius ( $R_{\star}$ ) range of $100-320\ {\rm R}_{\odot}$ , a hydrogen-rich envelope mass ( $M_{\textrm{env}}$ ) range of $0.07-5.16\ {\rm M}_{\odot}$ , a shock velocity ( $v_{s}$ ) range of $(0.84-1.60)\times 10^{9}\ \textrm{cm s}^{-1}$ , and a first light time offset (estimated difference from the time of first light given in Table 1, $t_{\textrm{offset}}$ ) of $0.000-0.003$ days. These parameter ranges likely reflect the variety of assumptions made across the different models, which we discuss in Section VI. The first ZTF $i$ -band detection point at $\delta t=0.027$ days likely captures emission from the initial shock breakout (as calculated in Section III.2). At this phase, the shock cooling emission models significantly deviate from the observed value (as seen in Figure 7). We explain further model constraints and our final selection of parameter ranges in Section VI.

## IV Spectroscopic Analysis

### IV.1 Optical

The evolution of the optical spectrum of SN 2024iss in the photospheric phase shows several key features (Figure 9). Early spectra up to $\delta t\sim 3$ days are featureless blackbody curves (A. V. Filippenko, 1997) reflecting a blackbody temperature peak in ultraviolet wavelengths. After 3 days, features from hydrogen begin to emerge, such as the characteristic P-Cygni profile (the combined absorption and emission features) of H $\alpha$ around 6500 Å. Prominent helium features, such as He i at 5800 Å, appear in early spectra after $\sim$ 5 days. As the photospheric velocity decreases, the H and He i features become narrower, with redshifted absorption features approaching the rest wavelength emission line. Fe ii, O i, and Ca ii features also appear in optical spectra after $\sim 20$ days.

We measured the spectral line velocities of prominent P-Cygni profiles that can be traced throughout the photospheric phase optical spectra ranging from $\delta t=4.0-94.9$ days (Figure 10). We calculated velocities using the absorption component minimum of the P-Cygni profile seen in each spectrum. H $\alpha$ appears to probe the highest velocities, starting at $\sim 18{,}000\ \textrm{km}\,\textrm{s}^{-1}$ and decreasing to $\sim 10{,}000\ \textrm{km}\,\textrm{s}^{-1}$ by $\delta t=90.4$ days. H $\beta$ and H $\gamma$ velocities follow a similar pattern, with H $\beta$ decreasing from $\sim 15{,}000\ \textrm{km}\,\textrm{s}^{-1}$ to $\sim 8{,}000\ \textrm{km}\,\textrm{s}^{-1}$ and H $\gamma$ from $\sim 12{,}000\ \textrm{km}\,\textrm{s}^{-1}$ to $\sim 7{,}000\ \textrm{km}\,\textrm{s}^{-1}$ . The velocity of He i evolves like that of H $\beta$ and H $\gamma$ , starting at $\sim 15{,}000\ \textrm{km}\,\textrm{s}^{-1}$ and decreasing to $\sim 7{,}000\ \textrm{km}\,\textrm{s}^{-1}$ . Fe ii displays a noticeably lower velocity than the elements listed above, starting at $\sim 8{,}000\ \textrm{km}\,\textrm{s}^{-1}$ at $\delta t=15.6$ days and decreasing to $\sim 4{,}000\ \textrm{km}\,\textrm{s}^{-1}$ at $\delta t=77.0$ days. This difference highlights various layers in the ejecta, with Fe ii $\lambda 5169$ probing the velocity just outside the photosphere (D. Kasen & S. E. Woosley, 2009; B. Paxton et al., 2018; J. A. Goldberg et al., 2019).

Optical spectra of SN 2024iss appear similar to optical spectra of other SNe IIb at similar phases (see Figure 11). The SNe 2016gkg, 2011dh, 2013df, 1993J, and 2024iss all show prominent features from H, He i, Fe ii, and Ca ii at $\delta t\sim 27$ days. SN 2024iss appears to have less pronounced Ca ii features at $\sim 4000$ Å and $\sim 8500$ Å , and more prominent H $\beta$ absorption compared to the other SNe IIb. No other distinguishable differences are seen between SN 2024iss and the other optical spectra of SNe IIb.

### IV.2 Ultraviolet

The $\delta t=7$ days UV spectrum contains blended features from several iron-group elements, causing ultraviolet flux suppression from line blanketing. This also makes it difficult to identify features from individual ions, since many of their signatures blend together (C. S. J. Pun et al., 1995; L. Dessart et al., 2008; S. Gezari et al., 2008; L. Dessart & D. J. Hillier, 2010; K. A. Bostroem et al., 2023). We have identified the features shown in Figure 12 from similar features in previous early-time SNe II UV spectra (S. Ben-Ami et al., 2015; S. S. Vasylyev et al., 2022; S. S. Vasylyev et al., 2023; K. A. Bostroem et al., 2023) and comparison to known prominent spectral lines. The SN 2024iss spectrum is mostly dominated by iron absorption from Fe ii and Fe iii. Additional iron-group metals with possible broad features include Mg ii ( $\sim 2800$ Å), Al iii ( $\sim 1820$ Å), Ni iii ( $\sim 1770$ Å), and Ti iii ( $\sim 2500$ Å). Narrow absorption features from the host galaxy interstellar medium can also be seen for Fe ii (2344 Å, 2383 Å) and Mg ii (2796 Å). We compared the $\delta t=7$ days UV spectrum to other early-time SNe II UV spectra at similar phases (SN 2022acko $\delta t=7$ days: K. A. Bostroem et al. 2023; SN 2023ixf $\delta t=8$ days: E. A. Zimmerman et al. 2024; SN 1993J $\delta t=9$ days: K. S. de Boer et al. 1993; G. Sonneborn et al. 1993; SN 2021yja $\delta t=9$ days: S. S. Vasylyev et al. 2022; SN 2022wsp $\delta t=10$ days: S. S. Vasylyev et al. 2023; SN 2013df $\delta t=13$ days: S. Ben-Ami et al. 2015; see Figure 12). We found that the SN 2024iss UV spectrum shows less prominent features than the other UV spectra. The SNe IIb (2024iss, 1993J, and 2013df) all lack distinctive absorption/emission features that are seen in other SNe II in the 2000 – 2500 Å range.

We measured the velocities of P-Cygni profiles present in the $\delta t=7$ days HST spectrum and compared the velocities from the UV wavelengths to those in the optical. We calculated the velocities using the minimum of the P-Cygni profile as seen in Figure 13, except for the velocity of the Mg ii emission line. Since the Mg ii profile is surrounded by other blended absorption features, we used the width of a fitted gaussian profile to measure the velocity. This resulted in an Mg ii velocity of $\sim 12{,}000\ \textrm{km}\,\textrm{s}^{-1}$ . From absorption features identified in the UV spectrum, we calculated velocities that may correspond to P-Cygni profiles of Ti iii ( $\sim 6{,}000\ \textrm{km}\,\textrm{s}^{-1}$ ), Al iii ( $\sim 6{,}000\ \textrm{km}\,\textrm{s}^{-1}$ ), and Ni iii ( $\sim 7{,}000\ \textrm{km}\,\textrm{s}^{-1}$ ) as seen in Figure 13. The UV velocities are consistent with H $\alpha$ , H $\beta$ , and He i velocties (identified from the optical spectrum) of $\sim 16{,}000$ , $\sim 14{,}000$ , and $\sim 12{,}000\ \textrm{km}\,\textrm{s}^{-1}$ respectively. However, due to the many overlapping transitions in the UV, the identifications of UV P-Cygni profiles are not definite.

### IV.3 Comparison to Early-Time Binary Progenitor Models

The hydrogen-rich envelope present at the time of explosion is a key differentiator between various subtypes of SNe II, and can be defined by the orbital period of the binary system (A. Ercolino et al., 2024; L. Dessart et al., 2024). We compared spectral models developed by L. Dessart et al. (2024), in which the mass of the hydrogen-rich envelope ( $M_{\textrm{env}}$ ) present at the time of explosion is a direct function of the orbital period of the progenitor’s binary system, to observed UV and optical spectra. The models assume a progenitor mass of $12.6\ {\rm M}_{\odot}$ , a companion mass of $11.97\ {\rm M}_{\odot}$ , a He core mass of $3.8\ {\rm M}_{\odot}$ , and a ${}^{56}\mathrm{Ni}$ mass of $0.09\ {\rm M}_{\odot}$ . More model specifics can be found in L. Dessart et al. (2024) and A. Ercolino et al. (2024), and the full grid of 10 models with corresponding parameters are listed in Tables 1 and 2 of L. Dessart et al. (2024). A shorter orbital period corresponds to more interaction between the progenitor star and its companion, stripping the progenitor’s hydrogen envelope and leaving less $M_{\textrm{env}}$ at the time of explosion. For orbital periods ranging from 562 to 2818 days (corresponding to a $M_{\textrm{env}}$ range of $0.00-6.86\ {\rm M}_{\odot}$ ), early-time model spectra were calculated using radiation hydrodynamics and non-local thermodynamic equilibrium time-dependent radiative transfer. We note that these models assume solar metallicity, which differs from the likely sub-solar ( $Z<0.6~\rm Z_{\odot}$ ) metallicity of SN 2024iss given its host environment. However, given the numerous metal lines in the UV and the high optical depths, significant effects in the model spectra would only be observed at extremely low metallicities of $<0.1~\rm Z_{\odot}$ .

We compared model spectra to the full HST $\delta t=7$ days UV to NIR spectrum and a range of early-time optical spectra (see Figure 14). The best-matched UV to NIR spectral model was the 2p85 model, corresponding to $M_{\textrm{env}}=0.19\ {\rm M}_{\odot}$ , $M_{\textrm{ej}}=2.43\ {\rm M}_{\odot}$ , and $R_{\star}=619.8\ {\rm R}_{\odot}$ . We note that the 2p90 model, which has similar physical properties, is also a closely matched model to the data but at a later model phase (Fig. 14). The 2p85 model, while being the best-matched, is still highly discrepant in the UV wavelengths. The deviation in the UV is likely the result of the model $R_{\star}$ being too large, leading to the model spectrum being overly luminous compared to SN 2024iss. Furthermore, there is no additional contribution from CSM interaction included in the model spectra and the effects of line-blanketing could be treated with more accuracy. The best-matched model for the optical spectra was the 2p90 model, corresponding to $M_{\textrm{env}}=0.28\ {\rm M}_{\odot}$ , $M_{\textrm{ej}}=2.49\ {\rm M}_{\odot}$ , and $R_{\star}=710.2\ {\rm R}_{\odot}$ . In the right panel of Figure 5, we compare the bolometric light curve of SN 2024iss to the model bolometric light curves of 2p80 ( $M_{\textrm{env}}=0.12\ {\rm M}_{\odot},M_{\textrm{ej}}=2.25\ {\rm M}_{\odot},R_{\star}=360.7\ {\rm R}_{\odot}$ ), 2p85, 2p90, and 2p95 ( $M_{\textrm{env}}=0.31\ {\rm M}_{\odot}$ , $M_{\textrm{ej}}=2.56\ {\rm M}_{\odot}$ , $R_{\star}=740.9\ {\rm R}_{\odot}$ ). The models do not appear to match the rise and peak phases for the observed 56Ni-powered curve in early times. This could be a result of the progenitor radius being too large in the model as well as the uncertain effects of 56Ni mixing/clumping in the outer ejecta (L. Dessart et al., 2018). After $\gtrsim 50$ days, the binary progenitor model light curves match the observed bolometric light curve and the nebular light curve model described in Section III.4.

### IV.4 Nebular Phase Spectra

We present the late-time optical ( $\delta t=259$ days) and NIR ( $\delta t=290$ days) spectra of SN 2024iss in Figure 15. In the optical, we identify prominent emission lines of [Ca ii], [O i], N ii, Mg i] and Fe ii, all consistent with expected emission from SNe IIb once the ejecta has become optically thin (i.e., “nebular”). In the NIR, we observe strong He i $\lambda$ 1.083 $\mu$ m emission as well as emission lines from intermediate-mass elements such as Na i and Mg i in addition to iron-group elements such as [Co ii], [Fe i/ii] and [Ni ii]. Given the lack of H emission at late-time phases, we compare the SN 2024iss nebular spectra to a grid of He-star models by L. Dessart et al. (2021) computed at similar late-time phases. As shown in Figure 15, the he6p0 ( $M_{\rm ej}=2.82~{\rm M}_{\odot}$ ) and he7p0 ( $M_{\rm ej}=3.33~{\rm M}_{\odot}$ ) model spectra provide a reasonable match to most emission line profiles at optical and NIR wavelengths. In the optical, we note that the model spectra over-predict the flux from Mg and Fe between 4000-5500 Å and under-predicts the He i $\lambda$ 1.083 $\mu$ m emission strength; however, the former can be remedied by additional clumping of the inner ejecta as shown in L. Dessart et al. (2021). In the NIR, the model under-predicts the line strengths of Mg i $\lambda$ 1.50 $\mu$ m and [Fe ii] $\lambda$ 1.64 $\mu$ m, but over-predicts the strength of [Ni ii] $\lambda$ 1.94 $\mu$ m.

In Figure 16, we present forbidden [O i] $\lambda$ 6300 and semi-forbidden Mg i] line velocities from low and medium resolution spectroscopy of SN 2024iss at $\delta t=259\ \&\ 412$ days. Overall, both profiles show significant structure e.g., the [O i] profile is double-peaked, with the bulk of the emission being offset to redder wavelengths by $\sim$ 580 km s-1 and can be well described by a Gaussian profile with a FHWM of $\sim$ 2600 km s-1. However, redward emission extends out to $\sim$ 6000 km s-1 and is not a monotonic function. Blueward of line center, the [O i] profile has a narrow peak centered at 660 km s-1, with FWHM of 1100 km s-1. Comparison to the Mg i] profile shows an identical line profile structure, but the redward emission does not extend to as high of velocities as in [O i] ( $\sim$ 4000-6000 km s-1). This line profile structure is suggestive of an aspherical ejecta distribution and/or ejecta clumping, as shown by L. Dessart et al. (2021) (see their section 7).

## V Circumstellar Environment & Progenitor Mass-loss History

The detection of luminous, fast-fading X-ray emission in SN 2024iss indicates SN ejecta interaction with confined CSM. In order to quantify the CSM densities that the shock samples at $\delta t<7$ days, we use the normalization of the X-ray spectrum to calculate the total emission measure (EM) at each epoch. Emission measure is defined as $EM=\int n_{e}n_{I}dV$ , where $n_{e}$ and $n_{I}$ are the electron and ion number densities in the emitting volume $V$ . We follow the procedure outlined in D. Brethauer et al. (2022) for deriving the unshocked CSM density, which is described by the following relation:

$$ \rho_{\rm CSM}(r)=\frac{m_{p}}{4}\left(\frac{2\times\rm EM(r)\mu_{e}\mu_{I}}{V_{\rm FS}(r)}\right)^{1/2} $$

where $\mu_{e}$ and $\mu_{I}$ are the mean molecular weight of electron and ion, respectively; $m_{p}$ is the proton mass; $\mathrm{V_{FS}}=\frac{4\pi}{3}f\left(R_{\rm out}^{3}-R_{\rm in}^{3}\right)$ is the emitting forward shock (FS) volume, with $R_{\rm in}$ and $R_{\rm out}$ are the inner and outer radius of the shell respectively and $f$ is the filling factor. We assume H-rich CSM with sub-solar composition ( $\mu_{e}=1.15$ , $\mu_{I}=1.24$ ), spherical CSM geometry ( $f=1$ ), and outer CSM radius of $R_{\rm out}=1.2~R_{\rm in}$ (R. A. Chevalier, 1982), where $R_{\rm in}=v_{\rm sh}t_{\rm SN}$ . Based on the H $\alpha$ velocities observed in early-time spectra, we adopt a range of shock velocities of $v_{\rm sh}=(1-3)\times 10^{4}~\textrm{km}\,\textrm{s}^{-1}$ when deriving CSM density estimates shown with respect to shock radius in Figure 17. Using these CSM densities, we make a rough estimate of the radiated luminosity from CSM interaction (i.e., $L=2\pi r\texttwosuperior\rho v_{\rm sh}^{3}\epsilon$ ) in Figure 5, assuming a radiative efficiency of $\epsilon=30$ % (D. K. Khatami & D. N. Kasen, 2024). Compared to the bolometric light curve of SN 2024iss, this shock powered emission could account for $\sim 10~\%$ of the luminosity budget in SN 2024iss at the phase of the primary light curve peak and $\sim 50\%$ during the minimum between both light curve peaks. This additional emission mechanism from CSM interaction at early-times likely influences the accuracy of physical parameters such as envelope mass and radius that are derived from shock cooling model fits (e.g., Fig. 8).

For $v_{\rm sh}=10^{4}~\textrm{km}\,\textrm{s}^{-1}$ , the CSM density profile can be fit with a steady-state ( $\rho\propto r^{-2}$ ) mass-loss rate of $\dot{M}=5\times 10^{-4}~$ M⊙ yr-1, for a wind velocity of $v_{w}=100~\textrm{km}\,\textrm{s}^{-1}$ . This value is chosen based on the velocities of unbound material found in 3D hydrodynamical simulations of SN IIb progenitor stars (e.g., J. A. Goldberg et al. 2026) and the likely compact nature of the SN 2024iss progenitor star based on the envelope radius and mass derived from shock cooling and the ejecta mass derived from bolometric light curve modeling. Nonetheless, it should be noted that much of the CSM in the 3-D simulations by J. A. Goldberg et al. (2026) remains bound and is not a steady-state wind-like profile. As shown in Figure 17, we compare CSM densities estimated from X-ray spectral modeling to the the pre-explosion density profile predicted by 3D simulations. While the simulations from J. A. Goldberg et al. (2026) do show elevated amounts of bound and unbound stellar material created by the star directly before collapse, the envelope densities derived from the range of shock cooling emission model parameters are higher than the average densities in the spherically-averaged 3D progenitor model snapshots for the YSG1L4.7 model. Furthermore, this simulation only traces CSM to $<10^{14}$ cm, which is not probed by the X-ray observations of SN 2024iss given that they occur at $\delta t>1$ day. However, as shown in Figure 17, the pre-explosion density profile of the larger 3-D progenitor model, YSG2L5.1, is consistent with the densities inferred from shock cooling emission and X-ray spectra modeling.

Also using the EM derived from modeling of the X-ray spectrum, L. Chen et al. (2025) find a lower mass loss rate of $\dot{M}=6\times 10^{-5}~$ M⊙ yr-1, but they assume a wind velocity of $v_{w}=10~\textrm{km}\,\textrm{s}^{-1}$ . Intriguingly, the deviation from a $t^{-1}$ decline rate in the X-ray light curve at $\delta t>7$ days indicates that these higher CSM densities, and enhanced $\dot{M}$ , do not extend beyond $R_{\rm sh}\approx(0.6-2)\times 10^{15}$ cm for $v_{\rm sh}=(1-3)\times 10^{4}~\textrm{km}\,\textrm{s}^{-1}$ . Assuming a progenitor wind velocity of $v_{w}=100~\textrm{km}\,\textrm{s}^{-1}$ , this corresponds to a phase of enhanced pre-explosion mass loss in the final $\sim 2-5$ years before core-collapse. However, steady-state mass loss may not be an appropriate descriptor of the circumstellar environment of SN 2024iss i.e., there could be CSM velocity gradients and/or not all the material is unbound. Overall, the CSM densities in SN 2024iss are too small for electron-scattering (“IIn-like”) emission line profiles observed in the early-time spectra of SN IIb 2013cu (A. Gal-Yam et al., 2014; J. H. Groh, 2014; G. Gräfener & J. S. Vink, 2016; L. Dessart et al., 2017) and some SNe IIP/L (e.g., O. Yaron et al. 2017; W. V. Jacobson-Galán et al. 2023; W. V. Jacobson-Galán et al. 2024).

## VI Discussion

### VI.1 Early Photometry

The rich, multiwavelength dataset for SN 2024iss probes the explosions’s underlying physical properties across a broad range of physical scales and processes, from the outer envelope and CSM to the explosion dynamics and bulk ejecta properties. With an initial ZTF $i$ -band detection at 1.3 hours after a $g$ -band non-detection, we obtained one of the most well-constrained times of first light for an SN IIb. By constraining the shock breakout regime to $\delta t<0.42$ days, we find that the $i$ -band point deviates from power-law models, making it consistent with shock breakout emission. Ultraviolet, optical, and near-infrared photometry displays the characteristic SN IIb double-peaked light curve. The shock cooling emission peak reaches a maximum at $\delta t=2.24$ days, which falls within the average shock cooling peak rise time range of $2.07\pm 1.0$ days for SNe IIb (A. Crawford et al., 2025). The early detection and well-sampled shock cooling emission peak of SN 2024iss demonstrates the need for early-time, high-cadence photometry to better explore shock breakout emission in SNe.

### VI.2 CSM Properties

The shock cooling emission peak coincides with exceptionally luminous X-ray emission up to $\delta t=7$ days, likely resulting from interaction between the SN shock and dense, confined CSM. With observed H $\alpha$ velocities, we consider a range of shock velocities from $(1-3)\times 10^{4}\ \textrm{km}\,\textrm{s}^{-1}$ . Assuming a brief episode of constant, steady-state mass-loss, this corresponds to a high progenitor mass-loss rate of $5\times 10^{-4}\ {\rm M}_{\odot}\ \textrm{yr}^{-1}$ with a wind velocity of $100\ \textrm{km}\,\textrm{s}^{-1}$ in the $\sim 2-5$ years leading up to explosion. However, as noted previously, the mass-loss in the SN 2024iss progenitor may not have been “steady-state” given the known complexities of the local environment of SN IIb progenitor stars (J. A. Goldberg et al., 2026). Previous X-ray studies of SNe IIb 1993J, 2011dh, and 2013df reveal mass-loss rates of $\sim 10^{-5}$ M⊙ yr-1(S. Immler et al., 2001; A. M. Soderberg et al., 2012; A. Kamble et al., 2016), placing the mass-loss rate of SN 2024iss at an order of magnitude higher than other SNe IIb. SN II 2023ixf exhibited emission consistent with a comparable mass-loss rate ( $10^{-4}$ M⊙ yr-1) to SN 2024iss, but with a lower assumed wind velocity ( $20\pm 5\ \textrm{km}\,\textrm{s}^{-1}$ ) (B. W. Grefenstette et al., 2023; P. Chandra et al., 2024; A. J. Nayana et al., 2025; W. V. Jacobson-Galán et al., 2025). In SN 2024iss, the high circumstellar density paired with a high wind velocity likely led to significant post-explosion CSM interaction. This resulted in excess emission that blurs the transition between the shock cooling emission peak and the 56Ni powered peak in the light curve (as seen in Figure 4). Modeling of X-ray observations shows that $\sim 50\%$ of the bolometric luminosity during this transitional phase can be attributed to emission from CSM interaction (see Figure 5).

### VI.3 Shock Cooling Emission & Progenitor Star Properties

The additional CSM interaction impacts the ability of models to explain the observations of SN 2024iss. Shock cooling models calibrated on supergiant progenitor characteristics (SW17 and MSW23) suggested a shock cooling emission curve lasting $\delta t=7$ days, while the P21 analytical model suggested a curve lasting $\delta t=5$ days. However, MSW23 was not calibrated for SNe IIb, a likely explanation for the inconsistent fits with UV photometry. Another likely culprit for the UV discrepancy is the shock power emergence from CSM interaction – this UV excess has been seen in other SNe IIb (e.g., 1993J, 2013df) and in UV spectra at later phases (S. Ben-Ami et al., 2015).

This study marks the second time MSW23 has been tested on an SN IIb, the first being on SN 2022hnt (J. R. Farah et al., 2025). As seen with our results and in J. R. Farah et al. (2025), despite MSW23 not being specifically calibrated for IIb SNe, it produces similar results to those of SW17 n=1.5. The progenitor radii from these two models, which are based on similar red supergiant progenitor characteristics (e.g., adiabatic structure of a fully efficient convective envelope), are in agreement with each other, giving an $R_{\star}$ range of $100-110\ {\rm R}_{\odot}$ . The SW17 n=3 model is based on blue supergiant progenitor characteristics (i.e., purely radiative envelope) and resulted in $R_{\star}=174.93^{+0.75}_{-0.74}\ {\rm R}_{\odot}$ . However, the corresponding $M_{\textrm{env}}=5.12^{+0.04}_{-0.03}\ {\rm M}_{\odot}$ is not realistic, since SNe IIb are expected to have stripped envelope masses of $\lesssim 1\ {\rm M}_{\odot}$ (M. W. Richmond et al., 1994; T. Matheson et al., 2000). This indicates that the progenitor of SN 2024iss is unlikely to be a blue supergiant star, so we disregard the SW17 n=3 results in further discussion. The P21 model, being fully analytical, is not calibrated on any specific progenitor type. Its resulting $R_{\star}=317.55^{+2.83}_{-2.90}\ {\rm R}_{\odot}$ and $M_{\textrm{env}}=7.45^{+0.05}_{-0.04}\times 10^{-2}\ {\rm M}_{\odot}$ may not be specifically calibrated to a progenitor star type, but are the statistically best fit parameters to SN 2024iss photometry. As a result, we consider the final $R_{\star}$ range to be $101-320\ {\rm R}_{\odot}$ and the final $M_{\textrm{env}}$ range to be $0.07-0.46\ {\rm M}_{\odot}$ .

M. Yamanaka et al. (2025) derived an $R_{\star}$ range of $50-340\ {\rm R}_{\odot}$ by comparing the photospheric temperature of SN 2024iss to analytic progenitor star models by D. Milisavljevic et al. (2013) and E. Nakar & R. Sari (2010). We find a more constrained $R_{\star}$ range through shock cooling emission modeling that is in agreement with theirs. L. Chen et al. (2025) obtained $R_{\star}=244\pm 43\ {\rm R}_{\odot}$ by modeling the shock cooling emission to $\delta t<5$ days with the SW17 n=1.5 model. While this fits within our overall progenitor radius range, we obtained $R_{\star}=106.31\pm 0.50\ {\rm R}_{\odot}$ with the SW17 n=1.5 model. One key difference is that we fit SW17 to $\delta t<7$ days, which we found was a statistically better fit than to $\delta t<5$ days (see Table 7). Additionally, the offset from the time of first light ( $t_{\textrm{offset}}$ ) is a free parameter in shock cooling emission models that impacts calculations of other best fit values. Due to our early ZTF detection, we have a much stronger constraint on this value, resulting in $t_{\textrm{offset}}<10^{-3}$ days, while the $t_{\textrm{offset}}$ from L. Chen et al. (2025) is $0.20^{+0.04}_{-0.06}$ days. As explained in Appendix A, we also place a stricter constraint on $f_{p}M$ (a parameter describing the fraction of ejecta mass related to the progenitor’s inner envelope structure) when using the lightcurve-fitting package. This allows for less uncertainty in estimated parameter values. Due to the tighter constraints and different phases for fitting, our hydrogen-rich envelope mass from SW17 n=1.5 ( $M_{\textrm{env}}=0.457\pm 0.003\ {\rm M}_{\odot}$ ) differs from that of L. Chen et al. (2025) ( $M_{\textrm{env}}=0.11\pm 0.04\ {\rm M}_{\odot}$ ) as well.

Red supergiant progenitors are expected to have their hydrogen-rich envelopes mostly intact ( $M_{\textrm{env}}\gtrsim 0.5\ {\rm M}_{\odot}$ ), but can evolve to yellow supergiants through mass-loss leading to a stripped hydrogen-rich envelope of $M_{\textrm{env}}\sim 0.05-0.5\ {\rm M}_{\odot}$ (C. Georgy, 2012; J. A. Goldberg et al., 2026). $M_{\textrm{env}}$ for SN 2024iss is consistent with that of a yellow supergiant progenitor. As seen in Figure 18, the SN 2024iss parameters are most similar to those of SNe 2011dh, 2024abfo, and 2013df, whose yellow supergiant progenitors were confirmed through pre-explosion imaging (M. C. Bersten et al., 2012; A. Reguitti et al., 2025; S. D. Van Dyk et al., 2014; A. Morales-Garoffolo et al., 2014). However, we caution the over-interpretation of this progenitor radius comparison given that this quantity is not derived through a consistent fitting procedure of the shock cooling peak across all of these works. R. A. Chevalier & A. M. Soderberg (2010) introduced two sub-classes of SNe IIb: extended envelope (eIIb) and compact envelope (cIIb). SNe eIIb are estimated to have $R_{\star}\sim 150\ {\rm R}_{\odot}$ and $M_{\textrm{env}}>0.1{\rm M}_{\odot}$ , while SNe cIIb are estimated to have $R_{\star}\sim 1.5\ {\rm R}_{\odot}$ and $M_{\textrm{env}}<0.1\ {\rm M}_{\odot}$ . Additionally, X-ray emission from SNe cIIb is expected to be predominantly non-thermal, while SNe eIIb X-ray emission is expected to be thermal. The radius estimate for SN 2024iss is consistent with that of an eIIb, the envelope mass ranges from cIIb to eIIb, and the thermal X-ray emission is consistent with expectations for an eIIb. This suggests that SN 2024iss is likely an SN eIIb, though we can not definitely constrain $M_{\textrm{env}}$ to either sub-class.

### VI.4 Progenitor Binarity

The leading explanation for the stripped hydrogen envelope of SNe IIb is the interaction with a companion star in a binary system leading up to the progenitor’s explosion (P. Podsiadlowski et al., 1992; N. Sravan et al., 2019; J. J. Eldridge et al., 2019; A. Ercolino et al., 2024; L. Dessart et al., 2024). In solar metallicity environments, the $R_{\star}$ , $M_{\textrm{env}}$ , and $M_{\textrm{ej}}$ of SN 2024iss are consistent with those of binary progenitor systems. The ejecta mass ( $M_{\textrm{ej}}=1.1-3.3\ {\rm M}_{\odot}$ ) is also inconsistent with that of a more massive single-star progenitor system ( $M_{\textrm{He core, preSN}}\gtrsim 9\ {\rm M}_{\odot}$ ) which would lose most of its hydrogen envelope naturally due to stronger winds (N. Sravan et al., 2020). In low metallicity environments ( $Z\approx 0.25Z_{\odot}$ ), the $R_{\star}$ , $M_{\textrm{env}}$ , and $M_{\textrm{ej}}$ of SN 2024iss are all inconsistent with a single-star progenitor system (N. Sravan et al., 2020). By comparing observed spectra of SN 2024iss with binary progenitor model spectra from L. Dessart et al. (2024), we obtain a $M_{\textrm{env}}$ range of $0.19-0.28\ {\rm M}_{\odot}$ , which is consistent with the range derived from shock cooling emission modeling. However, as seen in the right panel of Figure 14, the model spectrum shows some inconsistencies with the observed spectrum in the UV. This is likely due to the additional emission from CSM interaction, which strongly impacts UV flux but is not included in the models. Additionally, the best-matched models suggest an $R_{\star}$ range of $619.8-710.2\ {\rm R}_{\odot}$ . This does not agree with the $R_{\star}$ range from shock cooling emission modeling and likely leads to differences in the UV at early-time phases. As a result, we do not consider the values derived from these models to be definite constraints. L. Dessart et al. (2024) compared model spectra and light curves to observations of SN IIb 2011dh. For the yellow supergiant progenitor of SN 2011dh ( $M_{\textrm{env}}=0.1\ {\rm M}_{\odot},R_{\star}=200\ {\rm R}_{\odot}$ ; M. C. Bersten et al. 2012), the best-matched model was 2p80 ( $M_{\textrm{env}}=0.12\ {\rm M}_{\odot},R_{\star}=360.7\ {\rm R}_{\odot}$ ). Like SN 2024iss, $M_{\textrm{env}}$ from the model is close to other estimates, but $R_{\star}$ appears overestimated. However, the models appear to match more closely to observed spectra of SN 2011dh than those of SN 2024iss, highlighting the impact of CSM interaction emission on observations of SN 2024iss.

The SN 2024iss $\delta t=7$ days UV spectrum provides a unique snapshot of the outer layers of the supernova immediately following shock cooling emission, with likely contributions from additional CSM interaction emission. Numerous absorption features from iron-group elements result in heavy blanketing of UV flux and make it difficult to distinguish individual transition lines. We identified possible broad features corresponding to Ni iii, Al iii, Ti iii. If these features are genuine, they suggest that these metals are traveling at about half the velocity of the H and He i present in the outer ejecta. This is likely an optical depth effect that allows for slower moving hydrogen-rich ejecta with primordial Fe-group elements to be observed in the UV before these profiles emerge in the optical. Additionally, we detect a Mg ii feature at $\sim 2800$ Å with a velocity similar to that of H and He i. This places Mg ii with fast-moving hydrogen-rich material in the outer ejecta. Multiple UV spectra showing the evolution of absorption features through $\sim$ days/weeks in early phases would be useful for further investigating iron-group features in SNe II (E. A. Zimmerman et al., 2024; K. A. Bostroem et al., 2024, e.g.,).

Early UV spectra for SNe 2024iss, 2013df, and 1993J (all SNe IIb) lack distinctive features in the $\sim 2,000-2,500$ Å range. This contrasts with the other (non-IIb) SNe II in Figure 12, which contain several distinguishable emission and absorption features in this wavelength range. The lack of features could be attributed to additional line blanketing in SNe IIb UV spectra or the difference in hydrogen-rich envelope masses between SNe IIb and other SNe II. Since SNe IIb have less massive hydrogen-rich envelopes than other SNe II (S. Hachinger et al., 2012; A. Ercolino et al., 2024; L. Dessart et al., 2024), they may have less prominent emission and absorption features due to lower relative abundances. Additionally, SN 2024iss could have weaker iron-group emission/absorption features due to the low-metallicity progenitor environment. The possible distinctions underscore the need for a larger sample of early-time SNe II UV spectra, including those of SNe IIb, to better understand the source of any differences and their implications for ejecta properties and the circumstellar environment.

## VII Conclusions

In this paper we have presented X-ray/UV/optical/NIR observations of the SN IIb 2024iss located in a nearby dwarf host galaxy at $D\approx 14$ Mpc. Below we summarize the primary observational findings of SN 2024iss:

- 1. We present one of the best constrained times of first light for a SN IIb, with a ZTF $i$ -band detection at 0.027 days ( $\sim$ 40 minutes) after last $g$ -band non-detection. We find that a single power-law model fit to the multi-band photometry cannot reproduce the earliest $i$ -band detection ( $\sim$ 44 $\sigma$ deviation), suggesting an association with shock breakout emission. We constrain the timescale of shock breakout in SN 2024iss to be $\delta t<0.42$ days.

- 2. We obtained a UV spectrum of SN 2024iss at $\delta t=7$ days, which represents the earliest HST UV spectrum obtained of a SN IIb to date. In the UV spectrum, we detect possible iron-group features (Ni iii, Al iii, Ti iii), which had not been previously identified in any SN IIb UV spectrum. We find a stratification in the velocities of these iron-group features when compared to velocities of H and He i from optical spectra. We also identify a broad, blueshifted Mg ii feature with a velocity consistent with that of fast-moving hydrogen-rich material, tracing the fastest moving ejecta.

- 3. We find that the early-time UV spectrum of SN 2024iss displays considerably less prominent P-Cygni profiles of Fe-group elements than observed in SNe II-P observed in the UV at similar phases. This is likely related to increased line blanketing and/or lower metal abundances in the outer ejecta of SNe IIb compared to SNe II that arise from progenitor stars with less stripped H envelopes. Additionally, we observe an RMS deviation of $\sim 47$ % between SN 2024iss and a blackbody model in the wavelength range of $1600-2200$ Å due to increased emission from Fe-group transitions.

- 4. With shock cooling emission modeling, we constrain the progenitor radius to $100-320\ {\rm R}_{\odot}$ and the hydrogen-rich envelope mass to $0.07-0.46\ {\rm M}_{\odot}$ . These values are consistent with a yellow supergiant progenitor with a stripped hydrogen envelope.

- 5. We find that the best-matched model for a binary progenitor system corresponds to a stripped hydrogen-rich envelope mass of $0.19-0.28\ {\rm M}_{\odot}$ (L. Dessart et al., 2024), consistent with envelope mass estimates from shock cooling light curve model fits and other SNe IIb. The model is best-matched to observed optical spectra, but inconsistent with the observed UV spectrum.

- 6. We derive an ejecta mass ranging from $1.1-3.3\ {\rm M}_{\odot}$ , a kinetic energy ranging from $(2.3-6.4)\times 10^{50}$ erg, and a 56Ni mass of $0.11\pm 0.01\ {\rm M}_{\odot}$ from modeling of the secondary peak and tail of the bolometric light curve.

- 7. Using X-ray detections in the first week after first light, we estimate a CSM density of $8.4\times 10^{-15}$ g cm-3 at $R_{\rm sh}=1.8\times 10^{14}$ cm, which decreases to $1.1\times 10^{-15}$ g cm-3 at $R_{\rm sh}=5.9\times 10^{14}$ cm, assuming a shock velocity of $10^{4}~\textrm{km}\,\textrm{s}^{-1}$ . These CSM densities are consistent with a steady-state progenitor mass-loss rate of $5\times 10^{-4}\ {\rm M}_{\odot}\ \textrm{yr}^{-1}$ assuming a wind velocity of $100\ \textrm{km}\,\textrm{s}^{-1}$ in the $\sim 2-5$ years before explosion. The X-ray light curve, combined with the indicates significant luminosity contribution from CSM interaction between the shock cooling emission and 56Ni powered light curve peaks.

- 8. We obtained late-time optical/NIR spectra of SN 2024iss at $\delta t\sim$ 260-412 days, which are consistent with stripped-envelope SN models with $M_{\rm ej}=2.8-3.3~{\rm M}_{\odot}$ . Additionally, we identify multiple peaks in the forbidden emission lines of [O i] and Mg i], likely connected with inner ejecta asymmetry and/or clumping.

This analysis highlights the importance of ultraviolet observations for constraining supernova properties. Early-time and high cadence ultraviolet photometry is fundamental for accurately modeling shock cooling emissions and blackbody properties, and early-time UV spectroscopy provides new insights into the supernova environment during and after shock breakout. Upcoming UV space missions such as NASA’s Ultraviolet Explorer (UVEX, S. R. Kulkarni et al. 2021) will be key to furthering supernova studies in the ultraviolet.

## Appendix A Shock Cooling Models

The priors used for each parameter in the MCMC fitting for the shock cooling models are listed in table 6. The $f_{p}M$ parameter describes a fraction ( $f_{p}$ ) of the ejecta mass ( $M$ ) relating to the inner envelope structure of the progenitor (N. Sapir & E. Waxman, 2017). Shock cooling emission is independent of $f_{p}M$ (N. Sapir & E. Waxman, 2017; J. Morag et al., 2023). As a result, it is a free parameter in the lightcurve-fitting package (G. Hosseinzadeh et al., 2023) and a fixed value in the shock-cooling-curve package (P. Venkatraman & W. Jacobson-Galán, 2024). As seen in Figure 5 of N. Sapir & E. Waxman (2017), possible values for $f_{p}$ when n $=1.5$ range from $0.1-3$ . Since the expected ejecta mass is approximately $3\ {\rm M}_{\odot}$ , we limited our $f_{p}M$ MCMC prior to $0.3-10\ {\rm M}_{\odot}$ .

In order to determine the best phase to fit the shock cooling models to, we fit the SW17 n=1.5, SW17 n=3, and P21 models to photometry up to 5.0, 6.0, and 7.0 days after first light in the $i$ , $r$ , $V$ , $g$ , $B$ , $U$ , UVW1, UVM2, and UVW2 bands. We chose the fit with the lowest $\chi^{2}$ value as the best phase for each model. This resulted in the SW17 models being fit up to $\delta t=7$ days, and the P21 model being fit up to $\delta t=5$ days. We performed these fits using MCMC fitting with shock-cooling-curve (P. Venkatraman & W. Jacobson-Galán, 2024). The results can be seen in Table 7. Since the MSW23 model is based on the SW17 n=1.5 model, we fit it to photometry up to $\delta t=7$ days as well. Additionally, we compared our results for SW17 n=1.5 as derived from using shock-cooling-curve with the same model fit with lightcurve-fitting (G. Hosseinzadeh et al., 2023). We found the values to be very similar between the two, as seen in table 8.
